paragraphs.text: In another life, New Zealand pea breeder Adrian Russell would have been a forensic scientist. But these positions are hard to come by in New Zealand, and Russell drifted into a technical job specialising in legume* research for a government department in the 1980s. Forensic science’s loss has been pea growing’s gain. Today Russell heads a small plant-breeding team recognised globally as one of the best in a fiercely competitive international field. He can see certain parallels between his favoured and chosen professions, ‘At a genetic or DNA level there could be similarities, I suppose. Both are very much about observation, really. Most of the things you are looking for you can see if you look carefully enough. There are some amazing DNA diagnostic tools that can help, but mostly it’s about observation.”

His new pea variety, Aragorn, will soon be bound for the Indian sub-continent and South-East Asia. Due to be released this year in the United States, where it will be grown, it will be eaten as dry, split or gritted** peas. After gritting, the peas are made into Asian snack foods, while split peas are the main ingredient for dahl, a thick soup which is an Indian staple. Aragorn matures earlier, and is higher yielding, fruiting 20 per cent more per hectare than its successful predecessor, Cruiser. Like Cruiser however, Aragorn boasts a robust stalk, which means that the pea plants can stand up by themselves. Plants were selected and crossbred to produce this easily harvested plant.

Russell's company, Plant Research, has a US partner, Progene. This has meant that via an interactive breeding programme, trials could be held in glasshouses at both Lincoln University in New Zealand and in Washington State. This has halved the breeding time span of Aragorn and hastened its commercial release onto the market. But this arrangement is unusual, because of the big money surrounding horticulture, most breeding companies guard their secrets closely. Royalty income from the Aragorn variety should net Russell and his partners $1 million-plus over its average five-year lifespan.

After four years of development, Plant Research is now moving into a production phase of other legume varieties. Soon to be released are two semi-leafless marrowfat pea varieties. These will end up in Japan and South-East Asia as high-value snack foods. Their edge over other varieties is Russell's breakthrough breeding success: the ability for the peas to stay green over time. At this stage no other marrowfat pea variety has this same stay-green characteristic. “Both have improved green colours,” Russell says. ‘and this will give farmers a real advantage. At the moment they have to cut peas at an early stage, rake them into rows in the fields and let them ripen on the ground. If they leave them to ripen without cutting they can get bleaching because we have so much radiation in our sun that bleaches the chlorophyll*** in the grain. They end up looking white, which downgrades them as an export crop.’ Growers will find the greenness particularly attractive because bleaching can downgrade marrowfat peas to livestock food, reducing their value by as much as 30%. Their natural greener colouring will also be highly sought after in Japan because of regulations in that country which prevent artificial colouring.

As well as having a better colour, these pea plants are tougher so require fewer chemical treatments for damaging leaf diseases. While Aragorn was developed specifically for growing conditions in the Pacific Northwest, New Zealand growers will be given the first opportunity to plant the new marrowfat peas. One day they may be made available to the enormous growing nation of Canada and for this reason they will also be tested there. These peas would remove the labour-intensive need for Canadian growers to colour-sort their crops for days on end, and would give them big savings.

Yet another variety coming through is a maple pea for the niche domestic birdseed market centred in Europe. Resistant to pests such as blackfly and whitefly, this variety is being tested and a decision on its release will be made over the next two seasons.

The nature of plant breeding means that success stories are few and far between. According to Russell, ‘With plant breeding you have to get used to failure because 99 per cent of what you do is thrown away. You are only looking for that one plant in 10,000 – and the odds are probably even greater than that.’ Parent plants are carefully selected based on traits that breeders want to include in their new variety. These are crossed in a glasshouse and the resulting plants are screened in a time-consuming process over several years to the point where the traits are stabilised. From this stage they enter trials which measure both their performance and how much fruit they are likely to yield, to confirm the breeding results. Creating the perfect variety will always be elusive. When, as sometimes happens, a strain of a disease evolves which then rules out a particular plant variety, breeders go back to square one and come up with new resistance genes. Russell says the breeding process will never end. However, although plant breeding can be time-consuming and tedious work and does not hold the same allure as forensic science, it has its own rewards.
